title: When to stop: a dice game
objectives: Value a stopping game by backward induction.
Find the stopping threshold and see it rise with the rolls left
Link the rule to dealer quotes and early exercise of an American put

screens.title: Stop or roll again
screens.prose: You roll a fair die and win £1 per pip. After the roll you may stop and take it, or roll once more and take that second roll, whatever it is. Your first roll is a 3.
screens.question: Stop or roll again?

options.text: Roll again
Stop and take £3
options.why: A sure £3 feels safe, but a fresh roll is worth $\frac{1 + 2 + \dots + 6}{6} = 3.5$ on average.

options.text: It makes no difference
options.why: The two choices have different averages: £3 for sure against £3.50.

hints.text: What is a single fresh roll worth on average?
The six faces are equally likely.
A fresh roll averages $21 / 6 = 3.5$, more than 3.

feedback.correct: A new roll averages £3.50, more than £3.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare £3 with the average of a fresh roll.

byKey.stop: You kept the sure £3. Rolling again averages £3.50, so it is worth 50p more on average.

explain.text: With one roll left there is no decision, so that roll is worth exactly 3.5. Stopping is right only when the face beats what continuing is worth. Here 3 < 3.5, so roll.

screens.title: Where to stop
screens.prose: Same game: two rolls at most. Continuing is worth 3.5, whatever the first roll was.
screens.question: Tap every first-roll face you would stop on.

hints.text: Stop when the face beats the value of continuing.
Continuing is worth 3.5.
Faces above 3.5: 4, 5 and 6.

feedback.correct: Stop on 4, 5 or 6; roll on 1, 2 or 3.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare each face with 3.5.

byKey.six-only: You only stopped on 6. A 4 or a 5 also beats the 3.5 that rolling again is worth.
byKey.with-three: 3 is below 3.5, so rolling again is better on average.
byKey.r1c3: 3 is below 3.5, so rolling again is better on average.

explain.text: The rule is a threshold: stop on 4 or more. Each face is compared with the same number, the value of continuing.

screens.title: What the game is worth
screens.prose: Now price the 2-roll game before the first roll, playing the rule you just found.
screens.question: What is the 2-roll game worth on average, in £?

hints.text: Split on the first roll: you stop on 4, 5 or 6; on 1, 2 or 3 you get a roll worth 3.5.
Each face has probability $\frac{1}{6}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the stop faces, each times $\frac{1}{6}$, and the roll-on faces times 3.5.

byKey.one-roll: 3.5 is one roll. The option to roll again adds value.
byKey.stop-only: 2.5 counts only the stop faces. On 1, 2 or 3 you still get a roll worth 3.5, with probability $\frac{3}{6}$.
byKey.five: 5 is the average of 4, 5 and 6, but you reach those faces only half the time.

explain.text: $V_2 = \frac{4 + 5 + 6}{6} + \frac{3}{6} \times 3.5 = 4.25$, by the law of total expectation. We priced the last roll first, then stepped back one roll. Working from the end like this is **backward induction**.

screens.title: Three rolls
screens.prose: Now you may roll up to three times; each time you may stop. Your first roll is a 4.
screens.question: Stop or roll again?

options.text: Roll again: two rolls left are worth 4.25
Stop: 4 beats the average roll of 3.5
options.why: You compared 4 with one roll's value. Rolling on gives you the 2-roll game, worth 4.25.

options.text: Stop: a 4 is above the middle of the die
options.why: Being above the middle face is not the test. The test is whether 4 beats the value of continuing.

hints.text: If you roll on, what game are you left playing?
Rolling on leaves a 2-roll game.
A 2-roll game is worth 4.25, more than 4.

feedback.correct: Rolling on gives the 2-roll game, worth 4.25 > 4.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare 4 with the value of what is left, not with one roll.

byKey.stop: You compared with 3.5, the value of one roll. With two rolls left, continuing is worth 4.25, so a 4 is not enough.

explain.text: The bar to beat is the value of the game that remains, and it grows with the rolls left. With three rolls you stop only on 5 or 6. Comparing every roll with 3.5 throws value away.

screens.title: Value of three rolls
screens.prose: The tree shows the 3-roll game played well. Each leaf shows the average face you take there. Work from the right: the subtree after rolling on is the 2-roll game.
screens.question: What is the 3-roll game worth, $V_3$?

hints.text: You stop on 5 or 6 with probability $\frac{2}{6}$, worth 5.5 on average.
Otherwise, with probability $\frac{4}{6}$, you play the 2-roll game.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weight the stop leaf by $\frac{2}{6}$ and the 2-roll game by $\frac{4}{6}$.

byKey.v2: 4.25 is the 2-roll game, which you reach only after a 1 to 4.
byKey.no-opt: You used 3.5 for the roll-on branch. Rolling on leaves two rolls, worth 4.25.

explain.text: $V_3 = \frac{2}{6} \times 5.5 + \frac{4}{6} \times 4.25 = 4.6667$. Each node's value is an average of its children, computed from the leaves back to the root.

screens.title: One more roll
screens.prose: Extend the table to four rolls. With $n$ rolls, roll on the first one when it falls short of $V_{n-1}$.
screens.question: Fill the gaps.

columns: Stop on the first roll from

hints.text: The threshold for $n$ rolls is the smallest face at or above $V_{n-1}$.
For $n = 4$, compare faces with $V_3 = 4.6667$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare faces with the previous value, then average.

byKey.r3c1: $V_3 = 4.6667$, so a 5 beats it and a 4 does not: stop from 5.
byKey.r3c2: Stop on 5 or 6 (probability $\frac{2}{6}$, average 5.5) or roll into $V_3$: $\frac{11}{6} + \frac{4}{6} \times 4.6667$.

explain.text: 3.5, 4.25, 4.6667, 4.9444: each extra roll adds less. The threshold climbs from 4 to 5, and from six rolls on it is 6.

screens.title: Backward induction
screens.prose:
Every row of the table used one rule. With $X$ a fresh roll,

$$V_n = E\big[\max(X, V_{n-1})\big], \qquad V_1 = 3.5,$$

and you stop when the face is at least $V_{n-1}$. This is **optimal stopping**: compare what you get now with what continuing is worth, computed from the end.
screens.question: What happens to $V_n$ as $n$ grows?

options.text: It rises towards 6 but never reaches it
It settles back to 3.5
options.why: More rolls only add options, so the value can only rise. 3.5 is the value with no choice.

options.text: It grows without limit
options.why: You never win more than the largest face, £6.

options.text: It reaches 6 at $n = 6$
options.why: Even with many rolls left, the next roll could be your last chance, so $V_n < 6$ for every $n$.

feedback.correct: $V_n \to 6$: with endless rolls you wait for a 6.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. What does more choice do to the value, and what caps it?

explain.text: $V_n$ rises because more rolls never hurt, and it is capped by 6. $V_{10} \approx 5.65$ and $V_{50} \approx 5.9998$. The secretary problem is the same idea: pass on early candidates, then take the first that beats the rest.

screens.title: Write it
screens.prose: Write `dice_value(n)`, the value of the $n$-roll game, and `dice_threshold(n)`, the smallest face you stop on with the first roll of an $n$-roll game. With $n = 1$ you must take any face, so the threshold is 1. Stop on a tie.
screens.question: Write both functions.

widget.how: Check runs 12 hidden tests. Values are rounded to 6 places and compared exactly, so 4.666667 stands for 14/3.

hints.text: Start from $V_1 = 3.5$ and apply the rule $n - 1$ times.
One step: `sum(max(face, value) for face in range(1, 7)) / 6`.
For the threshold, compute `dice_value(n - 1)` and return the first face that is at least that.

feedback.correct: A loop of $n - 1$ steps from the last roll back to the first.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-3: Test 3 is $V_3 = 4.666667$. If you got 4.25, run the loop $n - 1$ times, not $n - 2$.
byKey.test-6: Test 6 is one roll: there is no choice, so you stop on any face, and the threshold is 1.
byKey.test-9: Test 9: with 5 rolls, compare with $V_4 = 4.9444$, not 3.5. Stop from 5.

explain.text: The loop runs from the end of the game to the start, which is the order backward induction needs. Each step costs 6 operations, so `dice_value(n)` is $O(n)$. By $n = 200$ the value rounds to 6.0.

screens.title: Why forwards fails
screens.prose: A colleague tries to value the 3-roll game from the first roll forwards, deciding each roll against 3.5. Put the correct backward computation in order.
screens.question: Order the steps.

lines.text: The last roll has no choice: $V_1 = 3.5$
With two rolls, stop on 4, 5 or 6, since each beats 3.5
With three rolls, stop on 5 or 6, since only these beat 4.25

hints.text: Which roll's value can you write down with no decision at all?
Every threshold needs the value of the game after it.
Value of one roll, threshold for two, value of two, threshold for three, value of three.

feedback.correct: Each threshold uses the value computed just before it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start at the last roll and step back.

explain.text: Going forwards, the first decision would need $V_2$ before it is known. Using 3.5 there instead gives the wrong threshold of 4, and a value of $\frac{4+5+6}{6} + \frac{3}{6} \times 4.25 = 4.625$ instead of 4.6667.

screens.title: Shopping a bond sale
screens.prose: You sell a bond by calling up to three dealers in turn. Each bids one of four prices, equally likely, independent of the others. Refuse a bid and it is gone; the third dealer's bid must be taken.

state.caption: Each dealer's bid per £100 nominal; a refused bid is gone

screens.question: What is the expected sale price with the best policy?

hints.text: Start with the last dealer: no choice, so the value is the average bid.
Last dealer: 99.4. Second dealer: accept 99.5 or 99.9, else take 99.4.

feedback.correct: Accept only 99.9 from the first dealer; the policy is worth 99.6375.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work back from the third dealer, as with the dice.

byKey.mean: 99.4 is one dealer. The option to call others is worth more.
byKey.two: 99.55 is the value with two dealers left. With three, take only 99.9 from the first.
byKey.first-best: You accepted 99.5 and 99.9 from the first dealer. 99.5 falls short of 99.55, the value of calling on.

explain.text: Take a quote when it beats the expected value of continuing: 99.9 from the first dealer, 99.5 or better from the second. Selling a house to a stream of offers follows the same logic.

screens.title: Exercising early
screens.prose: At one node of a binomial tree, an American put can be exercised now for £8.00. Its discounted, risk-neutral average over the next two nodes, the continuation value, is £7.40.
screens.question: What should the holder do, and what is the put worth at this node?

options.text: Exercise: the node is worth £8.00
Hold: options should never be exercised early
options.why: That is true for a call on a stock without dividends, not for a put. Here exercise beats continuation.

options.text: Hold: the node is worth £7.70, the average
options.why: The holder picks one, so the node takes the larger value, not the average.

options.text: Hold: the node is worth £7.40
options.why: Holding gives up £0.60. Exercising now pays more.

hints.text: This is the dice decision with different numbers.
Exercise is the face you have now; the continuation value is the game that remains.
Take the larger: £8.00 beats £7.40, so exercise.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare what you get now with what continuing is worth.

byKey.hold: You applied the rule for calls. An American put deep in the money is often worth exercising early.
byKey.avg: You averaged the two. The holder chooses, so the node takes the maximum.

explain.text: Each node of an American tree takes $\max(\text{exercise}, \text{continuation})$, worked from expiry backwards: our $V_n = E[\max(X, V_{n-1})]$. You met this in the trees course; now it is a DP over the tree.

ideas: Work from the end: the last roll has no choice and is worth 3.5. Each earlier roll is worth $E[\max(X, V_{n-1})]$.
Stop when what you have beats the value of continuing. The threshold rises with the rolls left: 4 with two rolls, 5 with three to five, 6 from six on.
The same comparison prices an American option on a tree and decides when to take a quote, an offer or a candidate.
summary.trap: Comparing every roll with 3.5, or working forwards, ignores that continuing is worth more when more rolls remain.

quiz.prose: A 1-roll game: you must take whatever you roll.
quiz.question: What is it worth, and is there any decision?

options.text: Worth 3.5, with no decision to make
Worth 6, if you stop at the right time
options.why: With one roll there is no later roll to wait for: you take the face.

options.text: Worth 3.5, and you stop only on 4 or more
options.why: Stopping on 4 or more needs a second roll to fall back on. Here there is none.

feedback.correct: No choice, so the value is the plain average: 3.5.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. What can you do after the only roll?

explain.text: $V_1 = 3.5$ is the base case: the last stage of every stopping problem has no decision. `dice_threshold(1)` is 1 for the same reason.

quiz.question: With five rolls, which first-roll faces should you stop on?

options.text: 5 and 6
6 only
options.why: 6 is the threshold from six rolls on. With five, compare with $V_4 = 4.9444$: a 5 beats it.

options.text: 4, 5 and 6
options.why: You compared with 3.5. A 4 falls short of 4.9444, the value of rolling on.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare each face with $V_4$.

explain.text: The threshold is the smallest face at least $V_{n-1}$: 5 here. Once $V_{n-1}$ passes 5, at $n = 6$, only a 6 stops you.

quiz.prose: You are selling a house. An offer arrives at £410,000. You estimate that waiting for the next offer, playing well from then on, is worth £402,000 on average.
quiz.question: What does the stopping rule say?

options.text: Accept: £410,000 beats the value of continuing
Wait: the next offer could be higher
options.why: It could, but on average continuing is worth £402,000. Compare with that average, not with the best case.

options.text: Compare £410,000 with the average offer instead
options.why: The average offer ignores that you could also refuse later offers. The value of continuing already includes that.

feedback.correct: Accept when the offer beats the value of continuing.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the offer in hand with what continuing is worth.

explain.text: £410,000 > £402,000, so accept. The rule is the dice rule: compare the sure amount with the continuation value.

quiz.prose: In the secretary problem you see $n$ candidates in random order and accept or reject each on the spot. You win only by picking the best. The optimal rule rejects about the first $n/e$, then takes the first candidate better than all before.
quiz.question: As $n$ grows, what does the chance of picking the best tend to?

options.text: $1/e \approx 0.368$

options.why: It feels as if a huge field must defeat any rule, but the threshold rule keeps a chance near 37% for every $n$.
That would need the best candidate to land in the second half and be picked every time. The rule sometimes stops too early.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The chance stays bounded away from 0.

explain.text: For $n = 100$ the best rule wins with probability about 0.371, and the limit is $1/e \approx 0.368$. Like the dice game, it weighs taking what you see against the value of waiting.
